reason: The sources robustly document the discovery, physical nature, and quasar-echo mechanism with multiple overlapping independent sites.
story: In 2007, Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel was classifying galaxies for the online citizen science project Galaxy Zoo when she noticed a bizarre, glowing green blob. Named Hanny's Voorwerp—Dutch for Hanny's Object—the structure spans the size of the Milky Way galaxy, roughly 650 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers quickly realized this eerie cloud of oxygen gas was shining without an obvious power source. The terrifying truth: it is a ghost image, or quasar light echo. Over 100,000 years ago, a supermassive black hole in neighboring galaxy IC 2497 ignited a brilliant quasar, blasting a beam of extreme radiation across intergalactic space. Although that monstrous engine has long since starved and switched off, its light beam is still traveling across deep space, illuminating the massive gas streamer in glowing green light. Gas flows from the dead quasar's host galaxy are now sparking new star birth within the cosmic ghost.
angle: A glowing green cloud the size of the Milky Way is actually the ghost image of a dead supermassive black hole quasar that switched off over 100,000 years ago.

claims.claim: Hanny's Voorwerp was discovered by Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel.
The object was discovered through visual classification of telescope images in the citizen science project Galaxy Zoo.
The name 'Hanny's Voorwerp' translates from Dutch to 'Hanny's Object'.
The object appears in close proximity to the spiral galaxy IC 2497.
Hanny's Voorwerp is located in the constellation Leo Minor.
The system is located roughly 650 million light-years from Earth.
Hanny's Voorwerp is roughly the size of a galaxy or the Milky Way.
The striking green color of the object is caused by emission from glowing, ionized oxygen.
The structure is an astronomical light echo or ionization echo illuminated by a nearby quasar.
The quasar responsible for the illumination was powered by a supermassive black hole in galaxy IC 2497.
The quasar that energized the cloud shut down or faded between 100,000 and 200,000 years ago.
High-resolution observations of Hanny's Voorwerp were carried out using the Hubble Space Telescope.
A central opening or hole measuring over 16,000 to 20,000 light-years across is visible in Hanny's Voorwerp.
Star birth is occurring in a region of Hanny's Voorwerp facing the galaxy IC 2497.
Gas flowing out from the core of IC 2497 compressed the gas in Hanny's Voorwerp to trigger star formation.
The youngest newly formed stars in the object are a few million years old.
The discovery spurred searches that identified a broader class of similar ionized clouds nicknamed 'Voorwerpjes'.

disputed: Discovery year: S1, S6, and S7 state the object was discovered in 2007, while S5 states 2008. Scripts should say 'around 2007' or leave the specific discovery year out.

Nature of the hole: S1 and S3 describe a physical opening possibly punched by a particle jet, whereas S2 suggests it may be an optical illusion caused by an obscuring shadow cast in the quasar beam. Scripts should describe it as an apparent hole or shadow.

Magnitude of quasar dimming: Early observations suggested the quasar shut down completely by multiple orders of magnitude (S1, S3, S4, S6), while later X-ray data revealed the core is partially obscured by dust and dropped in brightness by a factor of 50 (S5, S6). Scripts should state the core dropped dramatically in brightness rather than citing an absolute shutdown.
